name: How much extra should I budget for hidden structural issues?

mainEntity.name: How much contingency should I set aside for hidden structural problems during remodeling?
mainEntity.text: How much contingency should I set aside for hidden structural problems during remodeling?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hidden structural issues are common enough that a contingency budget should be part of every remodel plan. Older homes, homes with water intrusion, and homes with prior unpermitted work are especially likely to reveal surprises after demolition. The reserve should cover additional engineering, framing repairs, material changes, inspection delays, and any utility relocation that was not visible during planning. The right amount varies by project, but structural remodeling generally needs more contingency than cosmetic work because the risk of uncovering unseen conditions is higher. Instead of asking whether surprises will happen, homeowners should ask how the team will document, price, and approve them. A clear contingency plan keeps the project moving if the scope changes. It also reduces tension because the owner knows in advance that hidden repairs are a normal part of the process, not a sign that the contractor is mismanaging the job.
acceptedAnswer.description: A contingency budget is usually necessary because hidden rot, termite damage, outdated framing, or foundation issues can appear after demolition. The exact amount depends on age, condition, and scope, but structural projects should always include a realistic reserve.
